newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Austrian farmers reluctant bride in EU marriage.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Austrian farmers reluctant bride in EU marriage.

text.p: Discontent is rife among Austrian farmers almost two years after joining the European Union, but they grudgingly admit there is no other option open to secure survival in an increasingly threatened industry.

Most farmers vote for the conservative People's Party but the far-right is trying to pick up support ahead of Sunday's European parliamentary elections from voters in the country angry over a drastic slide in farm prices.

Max Fuchs, proud owner of 130 hectares (320 acres) of pasture and forest, has seen the price of beef plummet to 6.60 schillings ($0.613) per kg (2.2 lb) from 17 schillings before Austria joined the EU.
Milk prices have fallen by more than 30 percent.

"Things are black. If they carry on like this, our son will have to go out and get a different job rather than take over the farm," said Fuchs, on his mountain farm near the Styrian village of Gams in southern Austria.

The outbreak of mad cow disease in Britain was largely to blame for the fall in beef prices, but current EU payments of 3,440 schillings for his 17 head of cattle was a slap in the face, Fuchs said. "We used to get more support from the state."
"Many farms are closing down. You used to be able to live off 15 to 20 hectares (37 to 50 acres) of land -- now even 100 hectares (250 acres) is too little," he said.

At the other end of Austria, in the richer province of Tyrol, Josef Gasteiger said he voted to join the EU because he believed politicians' assurances that farmers would benefit from selling their produce to a bigger market.
"Now the truth is coming out. Look how prices have caved in," said Gasteiger, who now tries to make ends meet by renting out rooms to holiday-makers.
"Sadly, we're totally dependent on EU subsidies. But it's demoralising to produce products that are worth nothing," he said.
The Austrian government said that in 1995, the first year of EU membership, farming industry revenues jumped 22 percent.
But the far-right Freedom Party, which opposes Austria's big net budgetary contributions to Brussels, points out that a one-off payment for stock devaluation distorted the picture.
Farmers worry what will happen when EU subsidies tail off out and if ex-communist states in Eastern Europe join the bloc.
"I see no light at the end of the tunnel if eastern states like Hungary and Slovenia join. Prices will fall even lower and they'll need time to adjust to EU standards," said Fuchs.
"We're going to have to put more in the pot," agreed Gasteiger.
Many farmers in the lowlands of Austria have been forced to diversify from cattle farming to weather the price downturn. Pumpkins to make pumpkin seed oil guarantee high returns.
"Alpine farmers like me are the hardest hit. We can't switch -- with the gradient of my land, all the pumpkins would roll down into the valley," Fuchs said. ($1=10.77 Schilling)
